analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal workplace anti-harassment law and phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2024 and sent to five House committees, the bill never received a hearing, vote, or any action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen workplace anti-discrimination law in several ways: it would let workers recover uncapped damages for harassment, make a single incident of harassment enough to sue, extend civil rights protections to employers with as few as one employee, write protections for gay and transgender workers into statute, ban forced arbitration for discrimination claims, restrict nondisclosure agreements, and cover contractors, interns, and volunteers. It would also raise the subminimum wage for tipped workers from $2.13 an hour in annual steps until it equals the full federal minimum wage. Employers would face new requirements to adopt anti-harassment policies, run training, and pay fines for noncompliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — especially women, tipped restaurant workers earning the $2.13 federal subminimum wage, gay and transgender workers, low-wage workers who cannot afford a lawyer, and people in workplaces too small for current federal law to cover. Workers suing over discrimination would keep their day in court instead of being forced into private arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage in annual steps until tipped workers earn the full federal minimum wage, and confirms workers keep their own tips [S2].

Removes the caps on compensatory and punitive damages in federal employment discrimination cases and lets a single incident of harassment count as harassment, judged on the totality of circumstances [S2].
Extends Title VII protections to employers with one or more employees instead of 15 or more, and to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees [S2].

Writes into the Civil Rights Act that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is unlawful sex discrimination, including facility access consistent with gender identity, and bars religious liberty claims as a defense to Title VII suits [S2].
Bans mandatory arbitration of employment discrimination claims and restricts nondisclosure agreements, so workers can sue and speak publicly [S2].

Requires employers with 15 or more workers to adopt and post comprehensive anti-harassment policies, fined up to $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for willful or repeat violations), and funds legal assistance for low-income workers and a national harassment prevalence survey [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers. Restaurants and other tipped-wage businesses would pay higher base wages. Employers of all sizes would face compliance costs for policies and training, fines for lapses, uncapped lawsuit damages, broader legal exposure from a lower harassment threshold and one-employee coverage, and the loss of forced arbitration as a shield in discrimination cases.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small firms: covering employers with a single employee extends federal policy, training, and record-keeping mandates — and lawsuit exposure — to businesses that today fall outside the law [S2].

Removing damages caps and lowering the harassment threshold would raise litigation risk and legal and insurance costs for employers, costs that can be passed to consumers or absorbed in fewer hires, and the bill authorizes open-ended appropriations for the EEOC, Census, NIH, and grant programs without a price tag [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-side gains are substantial: a real wage floor for tipped workers and stronger, more usable legal remedies against harassment. The costs are real too — higher wages and compliance burdens for employers, heavier litigation exposure from uncapped damages and a broader definition of harassment — and the one-employee coverage threshold and the bar on religious-freedom defenses would draw serious opposition even from supporters of the bill's core goals. On balance the bill is designed to shift power and money from employers to workers, which is exactly why its path through a divided Congress was narrow.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 30, 2024, referred to five House committees the same day, and no committee ever scheduled a hearing or markup before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-MA) introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on July 30, 2024 [S1].
The same day it was referred to five committees — Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Accountability, and Veterans' Affairs [S4].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
The bill attracted 37 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republican support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly restaurants that pay the $2.13 tipped minimum wage and companies that rely on arbitration agreements — are better off, because they face no new wage, policy, training, or liability requirements from this bill.

against.name: House committee chairs (Education and the Workforce and four other committees)
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat with no action from referral until the Congress ended

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled House took no action on it

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill's fate was sealed by the Republican majority's committees taking no action; no Republican supported it at any stage.

industries.note: The bill would phase out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage until it reaches the full federal minimum, directly raising base pay for tipped servers. Restaurants have historically fought this change because tips currently substitute for most of their wage bill [S2].

industries.industry: Employers using mandatory arbitration and NDAs
industries.note: The bill would ban forced arbitration of discrimination claims and restrict nondisclosure agreements, removing tools that keep harassment disputes private and out of court [S2].

Employers would face mandatory anti-harassment policies and training, fines for noncompliance, uncapped damages, coverage down to one-employee businesses, and a statutory harassment standard that makes a single incident actionable — new costs, offset partly by clearer federal rules and free EEOC model materials [S2].

industries.industry: Civil rights plaintiff lawyers and legal-aid groups
industries.note: Uncapped damages, easier proof standards, and new federal grants for legal assistance to low-income workers would expand the demand and funding for worker-side representation [S2].
